utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in the courtroom. Could the witness be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to remind you that the affirmation you made yesterday to tell the truth still applies. And Mr. McCloskey has some additional questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning. Could we start where we left off? We had 6347 on the screen, and to remind everyone, the witness had testified about this. He had it from the original. He was looking at the original, and it was on the redirect issue of where he put his signature. And he also, you'll recall, testified that this appeared to him to be a typewritten document on the issue of how unusual typewriters or typewritten documents would be, as brought up on cross. And, Mr. President, it's now time to offer this into evidence. However, we don't -- oh, we do have an English translation, so I would offer this into evidence at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And now could we go --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P517.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we go to 6348. And if I could give the original -- if we could give the original of that to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Witness, and on the same issue as before, this document, as we can see, has "Ziza" up in the corner, so is this a "Ziza" document, not one of yours?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you tell, by looking at the original, whether that is a teleprinter or a typewriter used in making it?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Typewriter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And I would offer this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P518.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And staying with the issue on where you sign your teleprinter documents or other documents that you send to the teleprinter, I would like to just hopefully quickly be able to go through four documents to identify -- to see if you can identify your signature, so we can determine where you're doing it. If we could start with 6352. And I don't believe we have a translation for this. But can you recognise your signature anywhere on this?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So is that you down in the left corner?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's your normal signature, stating you sent a "predato" at a certain time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to 5914. And that last one will be marked only for identification, Mr. President, since it does not have a translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be marked, pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P519.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. So this is a -- we've given it a 65 ter number of 5914, and so we need a -- it does not have a translation, so we'll need a P number for that. I'm sorry, this does have a translation. I'm wrong about that. Can we go to page 2 of the B/C/S and page 3 of the English?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So do you recognise, sir, again your signature, and date, and "predato" in the left bottom corner of this document?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Would the witness please identify the handwriting on the upper right corner? What is written there, and by whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whose handwriting this is. All it says is "Very Urgent."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I would offer that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P520.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we can go to 6350. This has no translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, again, do you recognise the signature and date in the left lower corner of this document?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who is that?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how about the handwritten part of this document that finishes up the typewritten part? We see about four lines of handwriting. Do you recognise whose handwriting that is?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. That will be just marked for identification until we get a translation. Thank you. If we could go --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be marked for identification, pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P521, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the last document in this -- on this topic, 6351.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, sir, is that your signature, with "predato" and the date, in the left lower corner of this document?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we don't have a translation, so we'll be offering this later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P522, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, the next issue I would like to enter into briefly, I hope, is that -- it was first mentioned on page 2820, line 15, on cross-examination, and mentioned several times throughout, where General Tolimir was asking the witness about a perforated tape that the machine created to create a record of what was being sent. For another matter not related to this case, it so happens we did have -- we do have a teleprinter in storage, and I can wheel it out - it's right behind me - so that you can see what that is and get a little view of this thing regarding this tape, so you can get a better feel for what this machine is. It was never my intention to have him give us a lesson on the machine. I don't think that's necessary. But the discussion about tape was fairly extensive, so I think it may be a good idea just for you to see this. It won't take long. I also have a photograph of the machine, but unfortunately it didn't show the tape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Is this original machine one of those used in this specific office?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't believe so. This is just a machine we got from Bosnia, which I believe is similar or the same as the machine -- it may or may not be, but I believe it is. We'll, of course, have to rely on the witness. I've not shown this machine to the witness before. But whatever kind of machine it is, there is a tape that I think will help explain what the General was referring to, and it may assist the General's cross as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed as suggested. We would like to see the machine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If you could perhaps turn it around or put it to the side so the Court and the witness can get a look at the front of the machine. And I have a photograph of this machine. It's at 6357, so this can be the record of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Witness, does this machine look familiar to you, or this kind of machine, I should say?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You answered General Tolimir that you had two kinds of teleprinters at the Rogatica Brigade during your work there. Is this one of those kind?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And for the record, this is noted to be an ETL/1 machine, as we can see from the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I don't want to -- we don't need a lesson on this machine, but these two boxes sitting next to it that came with it, do you know what those had to do with, just very briefly?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you exactly, but I think that's where the transmission occurred. I couldn't tell you exactly how it works. I know that these two boxes came together with the teleprinter, but I couldn't explain how it works.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And as you testified, this teleprinter and its machines have the ability to encrypt messages when they were sent; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I'm sure you recall General Tolimir asking you about what he referred to as the perforated tape that left an impression and formed some sort of record of what was sent. Do you -- having his questions in mind, can you point out to us what you think he may have been asking you about?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the perforated tape of 15 or 20 millimetres. It's there [indicates]. When you type, some dots would appear on the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. And I'm not sure the Judges can see it, but we see paper through the plastic top of this machine, and what is that paper?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry. If you look down from the top of the machine -- if you need to you can stand up and take a look. Yes, that's what I'm talking about. What is that paper?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The paper would show what was being typed. As you type, the paper would show the letters. It's like a telegram, paper like this paper here [indicating].

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And you've testified that you used an electric machine, and is this, in fact, an electric teleprinter?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And one last question I have is: Do you recall whether or not this machine creates -- actually has physical arms that hit the paper and create the impression, or it's some kind of electronic impression, or is this an actual mechanical machine?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If you could, could you just look down at the top again and see if you see mechanical arms or anything that might help you answer that question? If the witness could --

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, they didn't quite catch what you said.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would you please say again what you said?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you just describe, after looking at the machine, what actually makes the impressions on the paper from this machine? Is it a mechanical arm or is it some kind of electronic printing like we're used to today?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's mechanical.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry to do this to you, but do you remember how to take off the top? And just take a look and maybe pull up anything you see. Just it's an issue I'd like to resolve.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And for the record, the witness hit the keyboard and then lifted it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you just tell us what it was you just lifted up, that metal piece you lifted up after pressing the keyboard?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could the camera zero in on this? Could the camera go off me and onto the machine, please? Can we get a frontal view so we can look inside the machine, please? The camera behind the Court would probably do a pretty good job. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And just one last time, could you lift up the mechanical arms that you lifted up briefly? Thank you very much, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, I would tender the photograph as 6357.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before we receive that, I would like to invite Mr. Gajic to have a look on the machine, so that he has, instead of the accused, an opportunity to see it directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have already seen the machine, so there is no need to do it now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The photograph will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P523.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, I don't have any further questions about the machine. I don't know if the Court does, but I'm done on that particular machine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In that case, it could be removed. Or there's no need to do that now. It could be done later, yes, to save court time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we go to 6356.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, you mentioned to General Tolimir that there was two machines. Does this machine look at all familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was this machine used when you were working at the Rogatica Brigade, this kind of machine?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I would offer this photograph of the Siemens T-100 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, it will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P524.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And could we bring up D49 on e-court. This is the 13 July document relating to people going to Sjemec, or proposing to send people to Sjemec. And could we show the witness the original typewritten version of that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I just want to clarify. If you -- let's get that up on the screen. General Tolimir was asking you about this document, and I believe it was up on the screen, and he asked you about the number which you had testified looked like "80" to you. Now that you look at the original document, where it says "Za 8" something, can you give us your opinion what that actual number is on the original document? Do you see where I'm talking? It's like the third line down, underneath --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How many zeros do you see on the original? I'm not talking about the computer. I mean the original.

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see one, and perhaps next to it there could be another 0. I'm not sure, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. President, I know the Court looked at this yesterday. I don't know if you want to look at it again. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, I would like to see it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. It should be shown again to the accused, if he is interested in it. Please carry on, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Could we now go to 65 ter 6349. We have a typed version and a handwritten version of the same document, and if both originals could be given to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this is on the issue of whether or not it was always the practice to sign -- for the author of document -- of teleprinters to sign the teleprinter or sign a handwritten version. Could we put these side by side so the Court could see both of them, since -- page 1 and page 2, I'm sorry. You'll see one is a handwritten version. There we go.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, first of all, looking at the handwritten version, do you see your signature under -- anywhere on this document?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then looking at the other -- the typeface document, do you see any indication -- your signature on that?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And for the record, on the handwritten document, the only handwritten signature we see is at the right lower corner.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is that you in the handwritten document?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And, sorry, back to the typewritten document, where do you see your signature on this document?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Top right corner.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we see initials "G.D." down in the left corner. Is that you, too?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, we don't have a translation for this, but are these documents related? In looking at both of them are -- and take a minute, if you need it.

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They're identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And which document would you have seen first?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This one [indicates], the one in handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what did you then do after receiving -- or what would you have normally done after receiving a handwritten document like this? I take it you don't -- do you remember this document at all?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would type it and then send it to the command of the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Just do you remember this particular document at all?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, when you -- so what is the left-hand document, the document that also has your signature on it, the typed version? Where does that fit into the process?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, if you got the handwritten document and typed it into the machine, what's the next document that would come as a result?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the same document, except it's typed up on the teleprinter. I don't know what else to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So is the teleprinter document the document that came out of the teleprinter after you typed the handwritten document into it?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you explain, do you know if you sent -- both are noted as sent. Do you think you sent this document twice or only once?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once, I think. But why I signed it twice, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we don't see any signature for Mr. Lelek anywhere on the handwritten document, do we? Take a look at it. Do you see any signature of Mr. Lelek or any other person that may have authored this document?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see any.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that's the same with the teleprinter document, there's no author that has signed off on that in handwriting, aside from yourself as the person that sent it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, there's only my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer this document to be MFI'd, because we don't yet have a translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be marked for identification, pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P525, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Just one last area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: On page 2877 of the transcript from yesterday, General Tolimir was asking you -- well, he asked you the following question: "If he met," meaning General Tolimir, "with Torlak at 12.00 and attended that meeting, was it then possible for him to write that telegram and send it to you from Boksanica by courier, having typewritten it as well, so that you were able to send it already at 1510?" Your answer was: "I don't know how long that meeting was. Boksanica is far away. And from Rogatica, I don't know." Can you tell us -- you've told us the Borike IKM, I think, was about 18 kilometres from the Rogatica Command. The Boksanica check-point, do you know where that was?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And had there been a telephone wire communication at Boksanica for General Tolimir's use, he could have or his -- a subordinate of his could have called the command directly and not used a courier; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if they had a telephone line from Boksanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's look at document P129. And if you could blow up just the paragraph right below the numbers. Thank you. And this is a -- we see a Ziza document, dated 14 July 1995, from the Rogatica Brigade Command. If we go to the end of -- let's go to the end of the document. It's the next -- well, there it is. "General Tolimir," in the B/C/S, I think we can see that. So if we go back up to the numbers 1 through 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this document, we see, it's sent to various places, including the Main Staff, the Drina Corps, the Drina Corps Forward Command Post, and the Command of the 65th Motorised Protection Regiment, and it's entitled "Placing the UNPROFOR check-points under our control." Then it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sorry, "under control."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, Freudian slip. And if we go down, we see short descriptions of the check-points.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then the paragraph right below number 10, it says: "There are currently eight soldiers and one APC at each check-point. For the time being, we have taken full control over the check-point number 2 at Boksanica, where the command of the UNPROFOR forces is located. We have wire connection with it. The check-point will remain functioning as if it is not blocked and surrounded by our forces." Does this help you remember whether or not there was a wire connection at the Boksanica check-point that General Tolimir had access to in July?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. There was a mistake in the reading. The word read out was "obradjen," "processed" -- sorry, "ogradjen" which means "fenced in," and the word really in there is "inspected," "toured," "obidjen," by our forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, we'll take a look at that, but the part about the wire connection is what I'm asking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Does that help refresh your recollection or provide you with any indication about this issue?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's of no help at all. I don't know if there was a connection, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, you testified you were in the teleprinter room. Was there a communications room or office at the brigade where they had a switchboard and radios that received the main incoming calls, both on the telephone and the radio, at the brigade?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was a switchboard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where was that in relation to where your building with the teleprinter room was?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just next to the teleprinter room.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did they have wire connections with you? Could the coms room pick up a phone and ring you so you would pick up and speak directly to them or whoever was calling?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of the time, we got out to go to the switchboard. It was just next-door to each other. There was no need to call on the phone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. I have nothing further, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Mr. Gojkovic, I have two questions for you, one a very simple one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We have heard very often the term "Ziza." What was the full name of this person?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The day before yesterday, the Prosecutor reminded me, because I had completely forgotten. His name was Desimir Zizovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And another part of the transcript of yesterday, I would like to clarify something. It is on page 72, lines 9 to 20. You were asked: "We have seen in all the telegrams that we have been shown so far that you wrote in the upper right-hand corner when you sent and received the telegrams that we saw on the screen and that we looked at so far; is that correct?" And you answered: "Yes." And now the relevant question. You were asked again: "Only in this telegram, we see that what is written in the left lower-hand corner is: 'Handed in at 1510 hours on the 13th of July, 1995,' and your signature, and that that is a photocopy of your signature and the words that you wrote in; is that correct?" And you said: "Yes." Do you remember these questions and answers of yesterday?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it would not be true if I said I really remember, but I can try.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Perhaps you can explain again what you were asked. If this signature was a photocopy, what did that mean, and why did you say "Yes"? I don't understand your answer completely. Perhaps we can have that part of the transcript on the screen again. I think it was the document P125. We could perhaps have that on the screen again to clarify this question in connection to the answer, the question of Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We do have the original of that, of course, and I think he had it in front of him when that question was asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. If you could give this original version to the witness again, that would be helpful. You were shown yesterday this document, and then you were asked if that is a photocopy of your signature and the words that you wrote in, if that is correct.

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is my signature. I don't know what I said was a photocopy. Maybe I was looking on the monitor and said that was a photocopy. This here is really my signature. Maybe I was looking at the screen at the time when I was saying that. I'm not sure if I had the document in my hand at that moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That clarifies the situation. Mr. Gojkovic, you will be pleased to hear this concludes the questioning for you, and you are now free to return to your normal activities and travel home. The Chamber would like to thank you for your attendance here and that you came again to The Hague. Thank you again, and all the best. The witness is now free to leave the courtroom. Thank you again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Ms. Chittenden is ready to go with the next witness, and I will be out for a moment with the machine and saying goodbye to the witness. So we're ready to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In your capacity as a technician, it's very appreciated that you remove this machine. Thank you. Good morning, Ms. Chittenden.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours, everyone in the courtroom. Our next witness today is Witness 117, who will be known as the pseudonym PW-050, and he will be testifying with face distortion today, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That means we should close the screens first --

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- so that the witness can be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Please stand and wait for a moment, and the screens should be opened. Again, good morning, sir. Welcome to the Tribunal. Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card which is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down. Ms. Chittenden is examining you, and I would like to remind you to speak slowly for the sake of the interpreters and the record.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: PW-050
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: We met this week. My name is Caitlin Chittenden, and I'll be asking you some questions today on behalf of the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Please, could we have Exhibit P504 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Witness, you'll see something coming up on the screen in front of you now. Please, could you read it to yourself and confirm that your name is written next to "PW-050"?

utterances.speaker: PW-050
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to tender this into evidence as an exhibit under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Witness, do you recall testifying in the case of Prosecutor versus Popovic on 7 March 2007?

utterances.speaker: PW-050
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Was your testimony at that time truthful and accurate?

utterances.speaker: PW-050
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Have you had the opportunity to listen to your Popovic testimony before coming here today?

utterances.speaker: PW-050
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: If you were asked the same questions again in court today, would you answer in the same way?

utterances.speaker: PW-050
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to offer the witness's testimony in the Popovic case into evidence at this time. It is P502, which is the under-seal version, and P503, which is the public version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time I would also like to offer three exhibits in conjunction with this witness's testimony in the Popovic case. The first exhibit is P497, under seal, which is the witness's OTP statement of 27 February 2007. This statement was admitted as the underlying 92 ter statement in Popovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, it will be received.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: The second exhibit is P498, under seal. This is the printed version of an intercepted conversation at 1057 hours on 19 January 2007.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: The third exhibit is P499, under seal. This is an attendance sheet from a page in the personal date book of PW-128 in Popovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This will be received as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, just to note --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: There is no translation of the letter document. Therefore it will be marked pending translation. Or do you have any translation?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: That's correct. There is no translation, because it just records names, but I can arrange for an English translation, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be marked.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, on the proposed exhibit list for this witness, you will also see P500, P501, and P505, all under seal. We have included these documents on the list for the purpose of assisting the Trial Chamber to make sense of the Popovic transcript. The Prosecution will not be seeking admission of these documents into evidence. Your Honours, I would now like to read a short summary of the witness's testimony in Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Witness, after I read out the summary, I'll have a few further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, if we may move into private session for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: The witness worked at the southern site until around November 1995, and upon its closure was reassigned to the northern site, where he worked until his demobilisation in April 1996. As a commander at the southern site, the witness was responsible for training and supervising his men in the use of radio equipment and the method of work. He described the procedure the intercept operators used to monitor radio channels, record conversations, transcribe those conversations in note-books, and type and transmit encrypted reports of these intercepted conversations. The witness personally typed and sent out these reports. The reports were encrypted and transmitted via the Paket radio system. The witness was the only typist in his detachment during January 1995, and up until around late 1995, when the unit moved to the northern facility. The witness stated that when transcribing intercepted conversations, operators were not permitted to draw inferences or to speculate. If an operator was uncertain of a word, the procedure he had to follow was to listen to the recording again with one or two colleagues. If none of the operators were certain of the word, then it would be marked intelligible [sic]. The witness stated that the reliability of the intercepts his unit recorded, transcribed, typed and transmitted depended on their accuracy and their timely dispatch. When the log-books, note-books, paper and tapes were filled, the witness would turn them over to his platoon commander or to the ABiH 2nd Corps. During his 2007 OTP interview, the witness reviewed two pages from the personal date book from the commander of the 2nd Detachment at the southern site. The date book indicated that this 2nd Detachment worked through until 16 January 1995 and then resumed work on 26 January 1995. During the intervening period between 16 and 26 January 1995, the witness stated that as the only other detachment at the southern site, the witness's detachment was automatically on duty. The witness also reviewed a batch of reports typed and sent from the southern site, including several reports from 19 January 1995, and he confirmed that he was on duty that day. For the record, these reports are marked as Exhibit 505, under seal. The witness further identified a typed report designated "03/1901" of an intercepted conversation from 1057 hours on 19 January 1995 and originating from the southern site and bearing his station number. The witness acknowledged that he typed and sent this report. For the record, this intercept report is Exhibit 498, under seal. Your Honours, that concludes my summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, this witness is the 1st Detachment commander from the southern site that we've heard from in this case, so I would just like to ask him about a few topics before we move to cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Witness, during the Popovic case you testified that as a commander at the southern site, you supervised the men in your detachment; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-050
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Can you briefly tell us what you did to supervise them?

utterances.speaker: PW-050
utterances.text: My tasks in monitoring the soldiers, the men who were under my command in the beginning, were to train them so that they would be able to work independently on the apparatus that we used to monitor enemy communications. Then the training did not boil just down to the manual use of the equipment, but also on communications principles, because I worked in the Yugoslav People's Army as a communications person, I was familiar with that, so I trained people that they understand the concepts of the communications so that they could then deal with some uncertainties and if perhaps something needed to be fixed in the communications. We worked in shifts. When I say "shifts," what I mean is the duty of a certain soldier at a specific post, his rest, when he needed to go for a meal, he needed to find a replacement to be there for him, when he was away, as well as the monitoring and control of their conduct at the work-place itself, whether they were conscientiously and properly carrying out their duties, that they're not missing certain conversations, because some conversations which might seem useless, for example, to someone, for example, a conversation by a member of the VRS with their wife or their son, while processing information, could provide some information that laymen would miss. So it was important not to miss any conversation, regardless of the fact whether it was a conversation on some military topics or whether it had to do with their personal life. Then we had to monitor the personnel during the transcription process, which means transcribing the material from the tapes to the note-books in handwriting. That was mostly the work and the monitoring of the soldiers during their work on the apparatus that we used to monitor the communications of the Army of Republika Srpska. In case when perhaps I was suspicious why a soldier would place an exclamation mark in the transcription process from the tape to the paper, I would replay that portion of the audiotape to see if there was something that made that soldier put the exclamation mark there. Sometimes it could happen that somebody would say a swear word as a joke. That could be one case. But sometimes this curse or some kind of objection would be uttered in a raised voice. Then that could be expressed by placing an exclamation mark. So I would go back and check whether this was said in anger and that's why the exclamation mark was there. We would check why somebody would put three dots at the end of the sentence. Perhaps I would listen to it again to make sure that those three dots meant that the person who was speaking stopped at that point and made a pause before he continued the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness, for that explanation. Can I gather, from your answer -- you were talking about reviewing a transcription with an exclamation mark or reviewing a transcription with three dots. Did you closely exercise supervision on your men? Were you hands-on at the facility, helping them?

utterances.speaker: PW-050
utterances.text: Yes. I personally didn't have a specific -- specific work hours, if I can put it that way. I didn't have specific duty hours. It wasn't logical, because I worked by myself on the computer to dispatch and encrypt dispatches. You never knew when a conversation would pop up, so my work hours were unlimited. I spent all of my time, including my free time, in one room where everybody was present, because it was unacceptable for at least one person to be there, other than the person who was supposed to be there on duty anyway. There always had to be somebody who could jump in as a replacement in case a soldier had to go to the bathroom or in case a conversation had to be recorded. Then the person on duty would transfer the conversation from the tape to the note-book in writing, and the assistant, who was ready, would sit at the apparatus and use the reserve recording operator -- apparatus and wait for the next conversation. So you always had to have somebody else present there too. I spent all of my time in that room, so -- except for when I was sleeping. I was there that whole time. And people would use the time when there were no conversations or when there was a lull in the work to find out how the antennas worked, to find out about some frequencies, 230 or 270 megahertz. Sometimes we would use that kind of antenna or another kind of antenna. I would explain to them what the point was in switching from one antenna to another. I would make sure that they wouldn't get too relaxed, and that while they were on duty, that they would be concentrated on their work in the highest possible degree.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Witness, you just mentioned before that you were responsible for training your men. Can I just ask a few specific questions? Did you train them in how to use the equipment?

utterances.speaker: PW-050
utterances.text: Yes. I already said that at the beginning, that that was the first part of the training, to teach them to operate the equipment manually that we used to tap the communications, how the frequency --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I interrupt you. Please slow down while giving an answer, because the interpreters and the transcript can't follow you with this speed. Please continue your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours. I apologise to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: I'd just like to move to -- I've just got a couple more brief questions. You have just been talking about the process of recording, transcribing, typing, and sending reports of intercepted conversations. My question is: During this process, did your men follow any established process or method of work?

utterances.speaker: PW-050
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Can you very briefly outline the steps in that process for me, just for the Trial Chamber, please?

utterances.speaker: PW-050
utterances.text: The procedure was for the soldier to sit at his post, with headphones on and paper and pencil ready in case a conversation occurred, any kind of conversation, any kind of sound in the ether. Then he would turn the recording device on to record the conversation. These were mostly UHER devices which were already connected to the radio receiver. And while the conversation was underway, he would follow this conversation. It was possible, if during the conversation a person was named or introduced themselves, then the person would write down who the collocutors were by first and last name. When the conversation was finished, he would switch off the recording device, he would call the duty officer, who would sit at his post, wait for the new conversation while this first soldier transcribe the conversation from the recording device. He would rewind it and then, word by word or two words, he would play and then pause, play and pause, and in that way transcribe everything into the note-book or piece of paper. The important thing was that the conversation was transcribed from the audiotape to handwriting word for word. In case a word was unintelligible or the person who spoke, spoke it too quietly or inaudibly or unintelligibly, at that time perhaps some interference in the communications happened. What the point was, was that this unintelligible word that one could not understand, in that case he would call one or two of the other operators to try together to decipher what that word was. I was called to do this many times in order to make the final decision. If it was absolutely unintelligible, then in parentheses you would always write down that that word was unintelligible. For example, if you could hear the first letter or two letters of that word and you don't hear the rest of the word, then in brackets you would put the remark "Unintelligible," first and second letters are such and such, and then the rest would be filled with dots. In case you couldn't understand two words, then you would say in parentheses "two unintelligible words said," without making any assumptions or guesses that it could be this word or that word, because any erroneous information to people who were working in automatic data processing could mislead them. After a conversation was transcribed, the conversation was replayed, checked again, and the handwriting was then handed over to me. Quite a few times, I had the habit, when retyping the handwritten text, to also check the audiotape because perhaps the soldier missed a letter or two, and in our language some words or some letters, you can steal some colloquial words. How do you steal them? For example, in English you could say, "What up," that kind of thing, and so also in our language you would have the same kind of colloquial language. So a word where a letter was missing at the beginning or at the end, I would check whether that was exactly like that in the audiotape or perhaps my soldier made that kind of error, which he was not supposed to do. In any case, I wanted to check every single detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I remind you again to slow down while speaking. And you were asked to answer very --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sorry. And you were asked to give a very brief answer. It was a quite lengthy answer. Perhaps you should take that into account, Ms. Chittenden.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Witness, I just have three more very brief questions for you. I apologise, if you could just answer them. I'm conscious of the time, and I would like to finish before the break, so we can finish. So, very briefly, can I pick up where you were talking about the operator bringing the handwritten transcription to you. When you typed it out, can you very briefly tell us what you did after that?

utterances.speaker: PW-050
utterances.text: After that, I would take the handwritten document, which is how we referred to it, I would use Editor and type it into the computer, because at the time we used the DOS platform, where the software was called Editor. And at the end, I would recheck the text to see if everything was typed in correctly, and then I would call up the programme for encryption of the document. Once the document was encrypted, I would call up SP 610 version software for the Paket radio which we used to transmit dispatches to automatic data processing.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Two more questions. In your experience, what would be the maximum time between the time the operator finished transcribing the intercept into the note-book to the time that you typed the intercept and sent it to automatic data processing at your command?

utterances.speaker: PW-050
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honours. I need a minute or two to answer this question. I'm going to try to be as brief as possible. It's hard to say how long it was from the transcription to the transmission of the conversation. That depended on the length and the intelligibility of the conversation. These were elements that influenced the time required. If it was a short conversation, let's say five or six lines in the handwriting, then the transcription, typing, and the automatic data processing was maybe five or six minutes. The length of time depended on the length of the conversation, the intelligibility of the conversation, how long the soldier needed to transcribe it, to check it, and to give it to me for me to type it. I apologise, Your Honours. I must mention that there were moments when some information that was exceptionally important, and information is as useful -- the more useful, the more it is sent in a timely manner. Sometimes I wouldn't wait to type word for word the text, but I would use the Paket radio chat mode and I would send them a summary in a sentence or two, informing them that a dispatch was picked up indicating that there would be shelling at such and such a place, for example, so that they would be able to inform such and such a location to issue an alert. Later, then I would transcribe the message word for word and dispatch it to the command. This would be done in order to save time and to dispatch the message before the shelling occurred.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I have one final question for you. If you can briefly explain, during the whole process, from the recording of the intercepted conversation to its transcription in the note-book, to when the operator brought it to you to type and send in an encrypted form, how important was it to be, very briefly, can you tell us, accurate in your work?

utterances.speaker: PW-050
utterances.text: It was extremely important. I think I've already said that the information is as valuable as it is authentic and timely. So it was very important not only to transmit it quickly, but to transmit it accurately towards the command, because belated information is valueless and inaccurate information is also valueless, because the people up there in the automatic data processing who made databases for certain units, certain movements, certain personnel, could be misled by any piece of inaccurate information.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Chittenden. We must have the first break now, and after the break, Mr. Tolimir, you may do your cross-examination. We must have the first break now, and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, before you commence the cross-examination, I have a question to Ms. Chittenden. We have received a huge list of exhibits marked for identification with P numbers, but you didn't tender them today. What are you doing? What is your intention?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the P numbers that I, sorry, intend to admit are the ones I read out. So I'm not sure if we have the same list. So it's P502, P503, P504, and P498 -- sorry, P497, P498, P499. And as I foreshadowed in my summary, I think P500, P501, and P505 are for your understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Then we have them on the record, but there are many others on the list, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: On my list, I just have those, but I apologise. Perhaps --

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: I just found out. Perhaps it was for another witness. I think there was a mix-up between witness numbers on the filing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: There were many discussions about exhibits not tendered yet, but perhaps I mixed up the two witnesses. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: I apologise. Those are the only ones for Witness 117. Can I -- may I also clarify something from the transcript?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: On page 24, line 11, I'm not sure if it was me misspeaking or something in the transcript, but it states "marked intelligible," and that should be "unintelligible."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just a moment. It was part of the witness summary?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: That is correct. So it was me speaking, and I think I may have said "intelligible" instead of "unintelligible." I'd like to clarify that for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, do you have cross-examination for this witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I greet all those present, and I wish that this day of trial finish in keeping with God's will, not as I want it to. And I wish all the best to the witness and everyone in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, since we speak the same language, would you please make a pause after each of my questions before you start answering.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we call up now, please, P497. Page 1, please, also in the native language of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We see here the statement you gave on the 22nd and 26th February 2007.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This should not be broadcast. Carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, tell us, please, where you gave this statement, and did you sign it?

utterances.speaker: PW-050
utterances.text: I see, on the English version, that I signed the statement, and it is indeed my signature. I gave the statement on the 22nd and 26th February 2007, but I really don't remember, Your Honours, whether I gave this statement by coming to the Tribunal or elsewhere. I think it was here on the premises.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Before coming here, did you have any contacts with the representatives of the OTP?

utterances.speaker: PW-050
utterances.text: Yes, I did have contacts with the OTP. Otherwise, I wouldn't be here. I wouldn't have been able to come if they had not arranged it, asked me whether I'm willing to come, and provided me with a visa.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: If you know the names, with whom did you talk from the Tribunal before coming here in February 2007 to testify?

utterances.speaker: PW-050
utterances.text: I can hardly tell you the names. Was the name Tomasz or something like that? I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Where was the interview made, and was it recorded?

utterances.speaker: PW-050
utterances.text: You mean talking to them before coming here?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-050
utterances.text: That first conversation took place in my place of residence, which I'm not going to name, and it was at 10-, 15-minute exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Is there a video or audio-recording of your conversation with that representative that you say was Tomasz?

utterances.speaker: PW-050
utterances.text: I didn't notice anyone turning on any recording device, video or audio.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us if you know the English language well enough to sign your statement only in English?

utterances.speaker: PW-050
utterances.text: I don't know the English language that well. But as to the second part of the question about signing a statement in English, I have great confidence in the people who gave the statement to me to sign, and I never for a moment suspected that anyone would mistranslate a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you look through your statement in your mother tongue, and is it identical to the statement in English, so that I can ask you questions based on the version in your mother tongue?

utterances.speaker: PW-050
utterances.text: From what I see, I don't see any differences.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Not on the first page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we call up page 2 of this document in both languages, paragraph 5. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I will read out to you just the first sentence: "When I was first mobilised, I was given the task to set up a radio station in" such and such a place "for the purpose of broadcasting public information." Can you tell me anything about what I've just read out? Is it true that you stated that? Is it correctly quoted?

utterances.speaker: PW-050
utterances.text: My first assignments, once I was mobilised, and in view of the fact that I'm a radio amateur, that I am also handy with electronics, I was contacted by a gentleman from my place of residence, who asked me, the way he put it then, to give him either help or instructions how best to set up a radio station in my place of residence. When I say "radio station," I don't mean a radio station for communication between two persons, but a radio broadcasting station, because by that time my place of residence was under an information blockade already and there was a great inflow of refugees, so a radio station was needed in order to broadcast news and information.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Who imposed that information blockade in your place of residence where you set up this station for public broadcasting?

utterances.speaker: PW-050
utterances.text: Who imposed the information blockade, I really don't know, but I know for a fact that the place where I reside was suddenly under an information blockade. And when I say "information blockade," I mean that we were receiving no information whatsoever either from television or radio. This place is geographically positioned in such a way that it is overlooked by a hill on which there was a TV transmitter, a TV repeater. Now, who turned it off and who stopped the broadcasting from the neighbouring repeater station, relay station, to our relay station, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Just tell the Court, was this relay under the control of the VRS or the BH Army, and which year it was?

utterances.speaker: PW-050
utterances.text: At that time, the place which is between my place of residence and the repeater was a village held by - I don't want to insult anyone by the terminology - held by members of the Serb community, and we had no access to the repeater. After a while, and I can't tell you how long exactly, that repeater fell under the control of the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us the name of that village, and is it currently inhabited by Serbs?

utterances.speaker: PW-050
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I say the name of the village in the location of the repeater, and I thank the gentleman for not telling the name of my place of residence, we were using the term "place of residence." If I identify the place, I will identify myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Should we go into closed session for a moment, private?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We don't need to go into private session. I can withdraw that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I just want the witness to tell me, if he can, if there are Serbs in that village currently?

utterances.speaker: PW-050
utterances.text: By now, there are again Serbs who have returned, whose houses have been restored.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us if during the war, when this repeater was controlled by the BH Army, there was any Serb population in that village?

utterances.speaker: PW-050
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: On page 8357 of the Popovic transcript, lines 11 and 12, you said you had conducted training for radio operators; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-050
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Whom did you train to operate radio equipment, and when?

utterances.speaker: PW-050
utterances.text: I trained soldiers who were in my section.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: On page 8359, lines 14 and 15, you said: "I did not have specific working hours. I supervised all the time." Also here, in examination-in-chief, responding to the Prosecutor, you said you supervised the work of soldiers subordinated to you, as well as their training. Can you tell us something about that?

utterances.speaker: PW-050
utterances.text: If I remember well, I said I supervised the work of my soldiers, that I didn't have specific working hours, that I spent most of my time in the workroom - that's how we called it - where the personnel and the equipment were, and, of course, I didn't sleep there. And during my sleep, of course, I did not supervise people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, you've answered my question. Now, tell me, on the days when you were resting, when you were not around, who sent reports? Because you said that you were the only one who typed, encrypted, and prepared messages for transmission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Ms. Chittenden.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd just like to say the witness didn't say on the days he wasn't there. I think that's a mis-characterisation of his evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: He said during sleeping times, he couldn't supervise.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: That's correct, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It has nothing to do with day or night-time.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: That's correct. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But you can answer the question, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to the gentleman, and the gentleman will understand me. I really have no intention to offend him, but he did say "on the days when I rested." In fact, when I was on duty on the south elevation, there were no days of rest. On leave, my entire unit would go to a place of residence with me to rest. When I said "during rest" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sorry, may I interrupt you. Mr. Tolimir asked you, in fact, who was sending reports during the time when you were sleeping.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While I was sleeping, nobody sent reports. If a conversation is intercepted, a soldier would wake me up, and then I would send a report. But that happened very rarely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, for helping us communicate.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: To be quite fair to you and Ms. Chittenden, I will read out from the seventh paragraph, the last sentence, where you say: "I was the only one who typed reports. The reports would then be encoded and sent in encrypted form." That's all I asked, who typed, because you said you were the only person who typed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I didn't mean to be disingenuous. I'm just asking questions to be of assistance to the Court.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't even try to say that you were being clever and sly, but there should be no playing with words. Of course, I couldn't sleep and type at the same time. I was interrupted a moment ago when I was saying that during the night -- and you know, yourself, that traffic was very rare during the night. It occurred mostly during the day. And if there was something, somebody would wake me up and I would send a report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We're going to move to a different topic. And now on page 8368, lines 5-8 from the Popovic case, you said: "I was absent only in September 1994, when I left for training, and also for New Year's 1995." Is that what you said then, do you remember - thank you - and is it correct what you said? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-050
utterances.text: The whole time that I worked on the northern -- on the southern location, the only time that I was absent -- when my group was on duty at the southern location, I was absent twice, in 1994, I think this was in September, when I went for training, and for the New Year's Eve festivities in 1995, beginning of 1996, because of my personal family problems. ^

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell me whether you had a rank when you were the commander of this department that you were managing? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-050
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. During the war, did you go for training outside of the B and H Army units?

utterances.speaker: PW-050
utterances.text: During the war, I didn't go anywhere for training outside the B and H Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And can you please tell us, did you go anywhere abroad, outside of Bosnia and Herzegovina, for training and education on these matters that we are discussing now, monitoring and surveillance of radio communications?

utterances.speaker: PW-050
utterances.text: I never went for any training outside of Bosnia and Herzegovina for the monitoring and listening in of communications. While I was active in the JNA, I did attend such trainings, actually not for monitoring communications, but for radio communications. But never outside of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You didn't answer my question about your rank. What was the rank that you held, please?

utterances.speaker: PW-050
utterances.text: I really cannot remember. This was the first basic rank as section commander. I don't know whether that was the rank of squad leader. I think, on the basis of that rank, I could only be in command of a squad.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And what was your training in Sarajevo that you referred to earlier? Did it have to do with eavesdropping that we are discussing now?

utterances.speaker: PW-050
utterances.text: Yes, it had to do with eavesdropping communications, surveillance. Other than, of course, training, I really cannot remember the name of that subject, but the basic content of that training was work with people, methods of working with people. It didn't have to be communications people exclusively. It could be other personnel, infantrymen. So methods of working with people, how to relate to people, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell us whether you were trained in the B and H Army by anyone who did not belong to the B and H Army but was from the ranks of some other army or force?

utterances.speaker: PW-050
utterances.text: Yes, I was. Your Honours, in order to avoid anybody from interpreting this in the wrong way, may I be allowed to clarify this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Believe me, I don't know the names of the people who trained us. I don't know if they were members of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina or not, because the training was done in civilian clothes, so I really cannot tell whether they were a member of the army or not. One of such trainers, I don't remember his name. I am not going to insult this person on religious grounds. His name was Mujica [phoen]. He died. He was a dedicated Radio Ham operator and was very knowledgeable in that area, and he gave us training on the types of antennas, diagrams of beaming, the angles of beaming, and so on. I assume that he was not a member of the B and H Army because he came to the training in civilian clothing. I knew him from civilian life, and he lived in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, thank you. This is quite a sufficient answer to the questions that I put.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you please directly answer this question: Were you ever trained by members of NATO countries or UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: PW-050
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In the Popovic case, you spoke a lot about automatic data processing units in the corps, and now, during the examination-in-chief - I took notes - you did also talk about the dispatch of Paket messages to the automatic data processing section; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-050
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. But I would like to make a correction. These are not Paket information batches. Information is something else. But the information was transmitted via the Paket communications method. These were encrypted documents, encrypted texts, that were sent to automatic data processing of the 2nd Corps Data Processing Section, via Paket.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. What I said was correct. Are you able to tell us a little bit more about this Automatic Data Processing Section to whom you sent the information you collected by eavesdropping on the communications?

utterances.speaker: PW-050
utterances.text: I can attempt to tell you what I know about that section. Sir, you have to understand that just like any army, our army, the Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, had some secrets, some data that should not have been known by everyone. As far as I know, the Automatic Data Processing Department was attached to the intelligence organ, and they gathered intelligence data. Our dispatches, the dispatches from the Anti-Electronic Warfare Unit from the northern location - I think that's the name. There were a couple of other locations. I don't need to mention their names. They gathered all the data, and that all was collected by the Automatic Data Processing Unit. The data was automatically processed, which means that they made a kind of library of data for specific things; for people, for units, how simply they would receive a dispatch from us. And then from that dispatch, they would pull out the needed information, and they would enter them into note-books, for example, where they would say, X or Y spoke with his wife. You could see that from one dispatch, the wife's name was such and such. From another dispatch, you could say that XX was the commander of unit YY. Then XX was a commander of some other unit. Then a new data library would be compiled with new information. So based on this information, they would create a kind of mosaic so that they have as many as possible useful pieces of information by unit as needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I think that was a sufficient answer. Can you please tell us whether you sent information only to that intelligence unit or did you also send your information to other users?

utterances.speaker: PW-050
utterances.text: The taped conversations were sent to the automatic data processing. Some information, I think I already mentioned, I think. If there was an order in the text about shelling, then I would use the Paket radio to inform a unit, if they also had Paket radio communications, so that I could let them know that they were going to be shelled. I would send the transcribed, encrypted, entire conversations to the Automatic Data Processing Unit, however. Some pieces of information that had to do with some other locations that came from a transcribed conversation, and that were not time sensitive, then the automatic data processing would send that nonsensitive information to some other units that would find that kind of information useful or that the information related to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In page 8379, lines 23 and 24 of the Popovic case, you say the following, I quote: "When I typed in a file, I would send it immediately to the Automatic Data Processing Unit, and what was left in my archive I would process in order to draw some conclusions." My question is: What conclusions did you draw, who did you send these conclusions to, and were they relevant only for you and for your own use or were they also meant to be used by someone else? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-050
utterances.text: I think that this was also in the JNA, and the same thing was in our army. I had the need for my own needs, not my own personal needs, but as commander of the unit I would have to pull up some information that was useful to me, so this was a partial data processing operation. In order for this to be clear to you and to the Trial Chamber, I'm sorry, Your Honour, that I'm taking up time, but I want to make sure that this is clear, that nobody misunderstands this. For example, if XX calls in to frequency 230 megahertz, this frequency would disappear the next day. Then I would search again, find him on frequency 240 megahertz. This is the type of information that I used. And, believe me, every army, every communications operator, would have in their radio station diary the working frequency, the reserve frequency, the call sign, the reserve call sign. This is information that I included in my partial data processing information, mostly because if I lost a contact, I would be able to search and find them again. I would already have the reserve frequencies noted down, so I wouldn't need to look for that again. I would type in those reserve frequencies into the memory, and one of those would kick in, and it would make my work faster and less complicated. So this is what this partial automatic data processing meant, for me to process data that would be useful later to me in my work.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you please briefly say, because of our time restraints, whether this processing of data you did on your own initiative or you did it upon the recommendation of your superior, and was this something that you informed your superiors about?

utterances.speaker: PW-050
utterances.text: It was my duty, as a commander, to process this data. Later, in a course for training in Sarajevo in 1994, we were also trained in methods of data processing. I don't recall that I had a written order with the signature of my superior to do this, but in oral conversations and conversations while receiving and handing over duty, the initiative was expressed that we also had to do this kind of partial data processing. But as I said, I don't recall having a written order about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you were the commander of an independent unit which was at the facility that you were in command of and that carried out the work you described, did you exchange information with any institution outside of the 2nd Corps and outside of the Automatic Data Processing Unit, or with any other service that was part of the B and H -- within B and H or outside of Bosnia and Herzegovina? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-050
