utterances.text: Any unit or military organisation outside of Bosnia and Herzegovina, definitely not. I didn't exchange information outside of my immediate circle of associates. It was quite a narrow area within which we exchanged, not data, this person said that and that. So we didn't exchange information about specific intercepted conversations, but we did ask for help from our neighbouring facility if I lost a frequency or if the signal became very weak. We had devices to measure the strength of a signal, and if this changed drastically, indicating that there were unfavorable weather conditions that damaged the signal, then I would ask a neighbouring facility to scan such and such a signal for its strength so that I would be able to proceed on the basis of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you please tell us here now whether that unit of yours, the Unit for Anti-Electronic Warfare, and you used that title yourself - that's what the unit is called - was it able to eavesdrop on forces of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Army of Republika Srpska, all the conflicting sides in the territory of the former Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PW-050
utterances.text: I apologise. I have to try to explain this to you. If our equipment was able to listen in on radio RRU 1 devices or RRU 800 which belonged to the Army of Republika Srpska, then I don't see -- I mean, it would be silly for me to say that these devices could not listen in to the same devices that were in the hands of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. But as far as I know, our army, the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, did not have -- perhaps it did have a small number of these devices. They might have had a small number of these devices, but we did not eavesdrop on our own units. If there was some witnesses who said something like that, perhaps, Your Honours, sir, in a different context, when there were war actions, combat actions, sometimes we would get an order to monitor our communications. But to monitor our communications, this is something the JNA did and what the members of the Army of Republika Srpska also did. They did it mostly so that they could point out to the responsible people in our own army that our communications operators were not carrying out their duties professionally, that they were being insolent with their work. The enemy forces, and I apologise for saying something like that, that the enemy could get information from them in the same way that we got information from members of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You've answered my question. Now, tell me, in this counter-electronic warfare, did you jam electronic signals or intercept signals only of the enemy or also one of your units if you noticed that they were leaking information?

utterances.speaker: PW-050
utterances.text: I don't recall that we jammed members of our own army. We did jam the signalsmen of the VRS, but I don't remember jamming our own communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us if you received any orders -- if you received orders for every instance of jamming or you were able to make the decision yourself to jam participants in radio traffic?

utterances.speaker: PW-050
utterances.text: You see, on the southern location we did not have jamming devices all the time. These jamming devices were sent to our location as required by the superior command in order to act upon intelligence that combat was about to start, and then these devices would be sent, on the eve of that combat, to jam the enemy signal. When we listened in on RRU 800, we didn't jam, because it was pointless to jam the communications from which we derived information. A normal signalsman is smart enough to realise that if he's being jammed, then he is also being monitored and intercepted. It would have been stupid on our part to jam the traffic which provided us with information. Jamming would mostly be done against hand-held radio stations, Motorolas that were used to communicate in the field. And even then, if we were able to make any use of that information, we preferred not to jam it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we call up P500.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: While we are waiting - you'll see this document shortly, it's very brief - it's your report dated 20th March 1995, and in the first sentence -- we still don't have it on the screen. There it is. Can you see now? Are you able to read? Could we enlarge the B/C/S version? Just in case, I will read it out to you when Ms. Chittenden finishes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: I'd just like to point out that this should be under seal, and so not broadcast. This is one of the exhibits we enumerated. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That's correct. The Registry is aware of that. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You say: "I hereby inform you that my Mini-Kobac has been installed and that I can now jam RTTY transmissions. "When I was told a few minutes ago to test the ability to jam frequency 258.275, the signal on this frequency instantly disappeared and has not returned. "I scanned the 232-270 megahertz range and found a new frequency of 247.075 megahertz, which was not registered during the scan last night. The strength of the signal on this frequency was 5 to 9 plus 20 dB on the S-metre, signal strength metre, the same as the signal at 258.275 megahertz." It's signed your name. I won't read it. Did you write this?

utterances.speaker: PW-050
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you install this Mini-Kobac radio set, and did you really engage in jamming, as this document shows?

utterances.speaker: PW-050
utterances.text: Sir, Your Honours, this is my document, bearing my signature, and indeed for a while there was a need to install this equipment to see, in the event things go out of control, how we would fare if we tried to jam these frequencies. That's the purpose of using this Mini-Kobac device. It was a device from the former JNA. It was also a transmitter, and it could cover this range, indeed, 230 to 270 megahertz. Just a moment. It says, "when I was told a few minutes ago to test the ability," so this does not refer to constant jamming. It refers, from what I see in my native language, to testing the ability of the device to jam. So I was asked to test. I tested, and then I reported on the findings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you are approaching the end of the given time for your cross-examination. You were told that this witness and the next one should finish their testimony today to enable them to return to their places of residence. You and especially the witness, you should be quite brief to finish as soon as possible. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, for this warning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, kindly refrain from giving long answers. Please try to answer my questions briefly, for the reasons stated by the Presiding Judge. Just tell me briefly, did you scan frequencies and participants yourself? Did the radio station scan automatically or you did it manually?

utterances.speaker: PW-050
utterances.text: The device, itself, did the scanning. You would press a certain button or turn a knob, and it would start scanning and stop at a frequency where a signal was discovered. The FM station is such that there is always a signal.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we call up page 3 of P497.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: That's your statement. And in the meantime, I'm going to ask you another question. We'll see here on this page that you referred to note-books, papers, tapes, et cetera, and how you turned it all over to officers of the 2nd Corps; is that so?

utterances.speaker: PW-050
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Tell us, please, did you ever, yourself, destroy such papers and note-books or tapes?

utterances.speaker: PW-050
utterances.text: I did, myself, erase tapes, always with prior consultation with one of my superiors from the command. We didn't have these tapes to burn, you know, so sometimes we were forced to erase tapes to re-use them. We mainly erased tapes containing irrelevant conversations like talks with wives or friends, conversations devoid of useful intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So in order to destroy something, you had to ask approval from your superior?

utterances.speaker: PW-050
utterances.text: For the most part, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Look at page 8 -- sorry, paragraph 8, line 6. One of the sentences reads: "Although I never saw hard copies, printed versions of these reports," et cetera, et cetera. Did you state this, and why, if so, do you say you were never able to see printed versions of these reports until you came to the offices of the OTP?

utterances.speaker: PW-050
utterances.text: Please let me find this passage and see in which context it was said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It's in line 6. It says: "Although I never saw printed versions of these reports, I recognised these reports as ones I typed and sent out on a daily basis to the Automatic Data Processing Unit myself." Therefore, I'm asking you: Is it true that you first saw these printed reports when the shown by the OTP?

utterances.speaker: PW-050
utterances.text: I think there's one thing you don't understand. There are reports and reports. There are reports about the condition and working order of the devices and equipment used at my location. I would type it up on a computer and send it, without printing it, so I didn't see the printed report. And when I went to the command, I never needed to tell anyone, Oh, please give me the hard copy of that report I sent earlier, just to see what it looks like. So reports of that kind, I never saw in hard copy because I never printed them for my own files. And whatever exchanges I had the command had nothing to do with the reports I sent. I talked about other things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Ms. Chittenden.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: I'd just like to clarify for the record that the batch of reports he's referring to, Mr. Tolimir, is P505, just to clarify. And if the witness would like to be shown that, but I'm not sure that that's necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'm not preempting anything. I'm just trying to understand what you are saying, because in response to a question from the Prosecutor, Ms. Chittenden, would you give the same answers to the same questions that were asked in the Popovic case, you said: "Yes." I read that from your statement -- from your evidence. That is evidence in that case. I'm just asking you again. Did you see any printed versions of your reports before you came to the OTP? Is it really true that you never saw your own reports typed up, regardless of the reason?

utterances.speaker: PW-050
utterances.text: I didn't see those typed-up reports in our own archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Are there at all in the archives of the BH Army any of your reports? Do they exist ? Did you see them before shown them -- before you were shown them by your own intelligence people or the OTP?

utterances.speaker: PW-050
utterances.text: I suppose they were filed, and they should be there. Archives are supposed to be kept for some time. Sometimes - and I don't know whether you have a copy of those reports that Ms. Chittenden just mentioned - there would be in the report a list of materiel and equipment, or I would write in a report I needed new batteries because the old batteries are used up. And when I came to the command the next time after sending such a report, I would say, perhaps to an officer, Could you please give me that report I sent, so that on the basis of it I could get these batteries.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I didn't ask you about correspondence between you and your command. I'm asking you about these intercepts that you mentioned. If that is your answer, I'm happy with it. We won't waste any more time. Is it true that you first saw them at the OTP offices?

utterances.speaker: PW-050
utterances.text: I don't know. Maybe out of a thousand papers, there was one that I really saw for the first time at the OTP. There were many papers in which I wrote to the command about the things I needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please, I have no ill intentions. You are a commanding officer, and I want to get information from you that I can use later when your underlings come here to testify. I need it to get insight into the work of your group at the southern location. Thank you for answering my questions. On behalf of the Defence, thank you for all the answers. Thank you for your fair treatment. Mr. President, I have completed my cross-examination. Thank you for your assistance, too.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for being fair in your examination. And all these blessings, I am not offended, although I am of different faith. And the gentleman knows that there is only one God, so no offence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for this very appreciated conversation. Thank you, Mr. Tolimir. Ms. Chittenden, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: I don't, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Witness, you will be pleased that concludes your questioning, your evidence for today. You are free now to return to your normal activities and to your place of residence. Thank you for your attendance here, and you are free now to leave The Hague. But please wait so that you are -- when you get up, you will be protected, wait for the screens to be shut down. Thank you again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may be excused. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Have a nice afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Welcome, Mr. Thayer. Mr. Thayer, is the next witness ready?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I believe so, Mr. President. I think he's a little under the weather, just to give the Trial Chamber and the parties a heads-up. He does have -- in addition to a flight he needs to catch, he has a doctor's appointment, I believe, at 1415. He arrived sick, and he's gotten a little worse. But he's fit to testify, as I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Then I would like to ask both parties to be very brief in questioning, especially the Prosecution, because it is a 92 ter witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We'll comply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before the witness is being brought in, I would like to raise a matter which I mixed up with the last witness. If I understand your information given to the Registry correctly, you will not use all the documents previously indicated with this witness. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I will not be showing those -- all those exhibits. If that is Your Honour's question, that is correct. There are one or two I will seek to show, but the rest I will tender as either part of the witness's prior testimony or in order to assist the Trial Chamber in making sense of either the Popovic transcript or the underlying Blagojevic transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And, in fact, all of them will be tendered -- in fact, they are already tendered by written submissions last year; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, with the exception, I believe, of two original note-books, the portions of which were shown to the witness in Blagojevic, but I would like to show him one of the original -- actually, both of the original note-books and offer those as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Good afternoon, sir. Please wait a moment so the screens should be opened first. Welcome to the Tribunal and good afternoon, again. Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card which is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, and now please sit down. There are protective measures in place for you. Your name will not be mentioned, there's a pseudonym, and your face will be distorted. I suppose Mr. Thayer has some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: PW-035
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I would just like to you look at your computer screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we could have P513 displayed on e-court, the pseudonym sheet.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I would ask if you could confirm to the Trial Chamber that you see your name on the computer screen underneath the code "PW-035."

utterances.speaker: PW-035
utterances.text: I can see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Is that your name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is my name.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Witness, do you recall testifying over the course of two days in this building in December of 2006?

utterances.speaker: PW-035
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you recently listen to all of that testimony which was in the Popovic case as well as your Blagojevic testimony?

utterances.speaker: PW-035
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you attest before this Trial Chamber that all of that testimony fairly and accurately reflects what you said during both trials, and in particular the Popovic trial?

utterances.speaker: PW-035
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Finally, sir, can you attest before this Trial Chamber that were you asked the same questions today that you were asked in 2006 in the Popovic case, that your answers would be the same?

utterances.speaker: PW-035
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution would tender P511 and P512, the witness's Popovic testimony, under seal and public version respectively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: They will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, at this time I'd like to read the 92 ter summary for the witness, and I think it can be in open session for its entirety. In the Popovic case, the witness's testimony from the Blagojevic trial was admitted as his 92 ter statement. A summary of the witness's relevant testimony in Blagojevic is set forth at pages 5455 to 5459 of the Popovic transcript, and the most relevant parts of the Blagojevic testimony, which was summarised in Popovic, are as follows: Prior to 1994, the witness worked as an intercept operator at the northern site, and in the spring of 1994, he was transferred to the southern site, where he worked until the end of the war. The witness did the same job at the southern location as he did at the northern location, and both locations used similar or the same equipment. The southern location was a higher elevation than the northern location, and, therefore, the received signal was clearer. To save a little bit of time, Your Honours, I'll skip the summary concerning the process and procedure that the witness employed to intercept, transcribe, and transmit the intercepts at the southern site. That process is summarised at the transcript page 5455 to 5459 of the Popovic transcript. And I'll just move ahead to save a little bit of time on that, but it's all there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, this kind of summary you have now done, by skipping the description of the whole process, is very well appreciated.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Hint taken, Mr. President. The witness recognised an intercepted conversation in his handwriting in intercept note-book 22, as well as a print-out of that transcript. He then identified two other transcriptions of the same conversation, which was intercepted by two other operators at another location. The witness then recognised a second intercepted conversation in his handwriting in intercept note-book number 103, as well as a print-out of that transcript. In Popovic, the witness noted that two lines from his note-book transcript were missing from the print-out. When the audio of that intercept was played in court, the witness heard the two lines which were missing from the print-out, but which he had, in fact, transcribed in the note-book. The witness also noted that in order to save time, he did not transcribe some of the preliminary conversation between Obrenovic and the operator and the first greeting between Obrenovic and Krstic, nor some lines which were repeated by the speakers. None of his omissions affected the meaning of the transcript, however. In Popovic, the witness further testified that sometimes he wrote the date in the note-book and sometimes he did not, and he was not troubled if he did not put the date in the note-book because he believed that the date was entered into the computer. The witness was also shown the original note-book 22. And when asked whether or not the following markings, "1 GEN 2001," was on the cover of that note-book when it was initially manufactured or whether it was placed there some time later, the witness stated that it was placed on the note-book when it was manufactured and that the intercept operators could not have done it. That concludes my summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, as I was looking at your Popovic testimony yesterday, I noted something in it that I didn't have a chance to ask you about, and I just want to follow up on one thing from the transcript that seemed unclear to me. And this is at transcript page 5464 to 5465 of the Popovic transcript. You were asked about comparing -- or you were asked to compare the note-book version with the print-out version, and your answer was: "My conclusion is that my handwritten version of this document resembles the other one and that the data is the same, the one that I wrote in my handwriting. And then there is the heading that we used to always put on that location on the computer, so this document resembles that format. And I can tell you that it is most likely from ..." And then you identify the southern location, and you say: "I can't confirm that with 100 per cent certainty but it certainly resembles that format." Then Judge Agius asked you a question, and he said: "You are using - or at least that is the interpretation that we are receiving - the word 'resembles.' Why are you using the word 'resembles' and not is exactly the same?" And then your answer was -- and this is where to me it is a little confusing in the transcript. Your answer in the transcript is: "I can tell you that my handwriting and this document are identical to some minor errors in the typed document." So I'm just asking you if you can clarify your answer there, just so that the transcript is fully comprehensible.

utterances.speaker: PW-035
utterances.text: Well, if I have time, I would prefer to look at the documents.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to speak up.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Probably it's not the same, because I dropped some words in the telegram, and the person who typed, when he types, he would call me or the person who actually received the telegram. Then we would agree, and then he would type in what I would read out to him. And probably I didn't read out or didn't manage to tell him -- actually, it was his task to call me if something was unclear to him, and then together we would agree -- or we would listen to the tape again. Then we would type up the conversation as accurately as possible so that he could send it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, could you please move a little bit further to the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let me ask you this, sir: Do you recall whether, at the southern location, you had the occasion to print out hard copies of the print-outs that you've been shown during the previous trials?

utterances.speaker: PW-035
utterances.text: I don't believe that I typed those documents during that whole period that I was there. I did substitute for the person who was typing because he couldn't or he wasn't there, but my documents were typed by another guy.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. My question was: Do you recall whether - let me put it this way - you ever saw a hard copy of one of these print-outs that you've been shown during the last trials, whether at the time, at the southern location, you saw hard-copy versions of the print-outs that were done on the laptop?

utterances.speaker: PW-035
utterances.text: I never saw that, because we didn't have a printer at our premises, and there was no need to do that, either, because all the printed documents were sent from the computer to our command.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, did you ever have the occasion to see one of these typewritten versions that we referred to as the print-outs? Did you ever have occasion to actually see it on the screen of the computer at the southern location?

utterances.speaker: PW-035
utterances.text: Yes, I had the opportunity to see that often. Even I typed the documents on two or three occasions when that person was away. I had the permission to do that, so I did do that plenty of times.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And based on those occasions, what can you tell the Trial Chamber about the hard-copy print-outs that you've seen in the prior trials and what you, yourself, saw on the screen of the computer, in terms of whether they look the same or look different, share the same characteristics or not? What can you tell the Trial Chamber about that?

utterances.speaker: PW-035
utterances.text: I can say with certainty that the versions that we printed were versions that I saw later when I came here during preparation for my testimony. These are the versions. We had special forms in the computer which we would use. We would change the date and enter our own data from the telegram. And these versions are identical to the ones that I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay, I'd like to hand you up a couple of items, with the usher's assistance, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: The first thing I'd like you to pay attention to is a blue plastic booklet. And just so you can avoid having to go through the English translations, I've placed little yellow stickies on the documents in your own language. If you could just look at tab 1 and tab 2, and tell the Trial Chamber what those tabs contain.

utterances.speaker: PW-035
utterances.text: The documents marked with yellow stickies -- well, this is a copy of the telegram, copied from the book that we filled in at my southern location. And this is my handwriting. I can recognise it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, could you indicate which P number --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- this document relates to?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: The tab 1 is P506, and tab 2 is P507.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if you could go to tab 2, sir.

utterances.speaker: PW-035
utterances.text: This is also a copy of the telegram from the note-book that we used at my location. I recognise my handwriting here as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And there should be an eight-digit number at the top of the page that's in your handwriting. If you could just read that into the record, sir.

utterances.speaker: PW-035
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Can you explain to me exactly which number?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If you're looking at tab 2, at the document that's in your handwriting --

utterances.speaker: PW-035
utterances.text: Yes. It's number 084430 [as interpreted], if that's the one you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: 00804430. And just for the clarity of the record, if you could go back to tab 1 again. That's the first intercept in your own handwriting. You've identified it as yours. If you could just read into the record what the eight-digit number is there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, I'd like you to look at the original note-book -- the original intercept note-book that you have underneath that blue packet. You were given two of them, and there's one that's marked "Note-book 22." This is P00440, for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: But if we could have P506 placed on e-court, please, for just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Before we start focusing on P506, I'd just ask you to look at the original note-book in your hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And why don't we put up P00440 while he's doing this, and we'll look at 506 in a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recognise what this is, sir?

utterances.speaker: PW-035
utterances.text: This is the note-book where we wrote down the intercepted conversations, where we wrote them down.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, looking at the handwritten transcripts which you wrote out, as well as the print-outs, can you give the Trial Chamber some idea approximately how soon after you intercepted the conversation, let's say the one that's in this book, which is the one behind tab 1, how soon after you intercepted that conversation off the airwaves did you take down that handwritten intercept? And this will be my last question before the break.

utterances.speaker: PW-035
utterances.text: This all depended on how important we thought the conversation was. It was important if new names of officers appeared, or if there was some orders that were important were there, or if there were some actions there by the enemy army, if some actions were underway, that dispatch or telegram would then be recorded first, depending on how long the conversation lasted. They had five, ten, fifteen minutes. Then after that, we would need approximately 15 to 20 minutes to transcribe everything from the audiotape, to copy it into the note-book that I'm holding in my hand. After that, if I concluded that this was a more important conversation, I would call the person, if he wasn't already in the room, who was entrusted with typing it into the computer. I would dictate; he would type. He also needed some 15 minutes or so to type it all in. And then when he was finished, he would send it, after encryption, to the command. So that would be the time from the receipt to the transmission of a particular telegram.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand it's a convenient time for the second break. We must, on technical reasons, now have the second break. We adjourn and resume five past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Witness, I'm going to cut my examination further to make sure you get out of here on time.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: The first thing I'd like to put up on the screen is P00440. That's the original note-book number 22.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, I'd ask you to take a look at the original note-book that you have there before you, that's marked with the number 22 and which has the intercept that you spoke about earlier at tab 1 of your booklet, just for the record, Colonel Beara complaining to General Krstic that Furtula didn't carry out the boss's order. Sir, if you could, just look at the cover, please, of that note-book.

utterances.speaker: PW-035
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: In the Popovic case, you were asked by the attorney for Colonel Beara about the notations -- the markings that we see on the cover there. It's a phrase which is repeated, "1 GEN 2001." We can see it. They run horizontally and vertically, if we're looking on the screen here. And you were specifically asked by the lawyer for Colonel Beara, in the last trial, whether you or any of your intercept operators/colleagues placed those markings on there or whether that note-book was produced or manufactured with those phrases on the cover. Do you recall that, those questions and your answers, sir?

utterances.speaker: PW-035
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that question. I also remember the answer. Now, when I look at this line and these numbers here again, I'm still thinking it's the university group, that they were meeting again after 10 years, or some other anniversary, just like we do. Those who were using this note-book, they put it in, this "1st Generation 2001." That's what it could mean. At least that's what I suppose. If we -- we wouldn't have done that ourselves this time. I believe these numbers and letters are part of the note-book itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And when you're referring to the university group, I take it you're referring to this pink animal. I respectfully disagree with my colleague, Mr. Vanderpuye. He's identified it as a chipmunk. I firmly believe that is a pink bear on the cover. But I presume that is who you are referring to, sir. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-035
utterances.text: Yes, I mean this picture, a pink bear, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, it has been suggested, sir, that these markings indicate that what is written inside that note-book was not written at the time these intercepts were taken, that is, in July of 1995, and that, in fact, this note-book and others were fabricated later, after the relevant time-period in this case. What do you have to say to the Trial Chamber about that suggestion, sir?

utterances.speaker: PW-035
utterances.text: I can only say that it would be silly.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And would it change your testimony, sir, if someone came into court and showed you an expert report that concluded that the note-book that you're holding was fabricated, in terms of its contents, that those intercept -- handwritten intercept transcripts in there were put in there after July 1995? Would it make a difference to your testimony if someone showed you an expert report that came to that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: PW-035
utterances.text: No difference, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, with the usher's assistance, I would just like to show you two more documents very quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And could the original note-book the witness was testifying about be shown to the Chamber and to Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Absolutely, Mr. President. And I believe you've seen the pink bear before, and I'll be happy to hand it up again for your inspection and for the accused's inspection.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, do you recall testifying in the Blagojevic case about two other intercept operators who also captured the conversation which you wrote down about Colonel Beara complaining to General Krstic that he didn't have enough men? Do you recall being shown excerpts from two other note-books in the Blagojevic case from two other intercept operators who also listened to that same conversation and who noted slightly different times? Do you remember that testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: PW-035
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, if you would look at the note-book that's marked "91," and there's a green sticky on one of the pages. And for e-court purposes, that is 506 -- P506E. Can you tell the Trial Chamber what we're looking at? There's a time of 0957 hours in the upper left-hand corner. Just briefly, what is this?

utterances.speaker: PW-035
utterances.text: It's the time when the tape-recorder was turned on to record this conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recognise the content of this conversation?

utterances.speaker: PW-035
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: What does it appear to you to be?

utterances.speaker: PW-035
utterances.text: It's the same intercept, identical to the one I intercepted at the southern location.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And we see here that only one side of the conversation has been recorded. Can you just very briefly tell the Trial Chamber -- based on your experience, can you explain the difference between what you heard and what this other operator heard?

utterances.speaker: PW-035
utterances.text: I can. It happened not once; it happened quite often. My location was more elevated by about 400 metres, and that's one of the reasons why we were able to hear both ends of the conversation with a louder signal and a clearer signal. The location that intercepted this is by 400 metres lower, and it's possible they did not have a good line towards the antennas and the transmitters used by these gentlemen who are talking. That means that if the eavesdropping device is not in the same line as the antenna, the signal can be heard very feebly, especially if the location is lower. With my location, you don't even need a straight line.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Witness. Now, if you would put that note-book to the side for a moment. And you worked at both the northern and southern locations. Let me just ask you: The original note-book that you have there that's marked number 91, and the one that's underneath it that's marked number 24, are those the same types of note-books that you used at both locations, sir?

utterances.speaker: PW-035
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, very quickly, if you could pick up the one that's marked number 24. That's the other one that you have there. And if we could look at P506G, please. And I just turn your attention to a tabbed page.

utterances.speaker: PW-035
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you see an intercept with the time of 0955 hours?

utterances.speaker: PW-035
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what is that, sir? What does it appear to you to be?

utterances.speaker: PW-035
utterances.text: It appears to be the same intercept, the same conversation I intercepted, with slight differences. The participants in the conversation are the same, the time is more or less the same, with the difference of a couple of minutes, the same frequency, so it must be the same conversation that I intercepted and noted down in my note-book.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And was that operator able to intercept the entire conversation, sir?

utterances.speaker: PW-035
utterances.text: Most of it, yes. I even see here X and dots, which means that he was not able to receive that, but he did receive a lot of it from both ends of the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Witness. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: To save time, Mr. President, perhaps the tendering could be postponed until later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, that is a very good suggestion. I have to apologise, especially for Mr. Tolimir, that I was five minutes delayed because of another commitment. But we can sit until 10 minutes before 2.00. Mr. Tolimir, do you have cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. My greetings to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: If you have a problem, because I have heard that you have seen a doctor, I can give up on this cross-examination so you don't need to come back. Just tell me if you are able to answer questions. If you are, I will ask a couple of questions, because we can get the same answers by questioning some of your colleagues.

utterances.speaker: PW-035
utterances.text: It's okay that you continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I will then pick up from the same document shown to you before, 506.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If it can be brought back up, and I'll try to make it quick. 506 is the document for e-court, and there is a letter G. It was on the screen a moment ago. I can see it. Could you now show the same conversation as intercepted by the other operator, P506B. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We can see both conversations now on the screen, both intercepts, and I'd like to ask: Did you turn on your tape-recorder at 9.55, the same as the other operator?

utterances.speaker: PW-035
utterances.text: I turned on my tape-recorder at the time that I recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: What is that time, for the record?

utterances.speaker: PW-035
utterances.text: If I remember well, it was 9.57.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And what's written on this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Somebody removed the document, but never mind. This time difference of five minutes, could it be waiting or could it account for the difference of a few words between the intercepts of the other operator and yours?

utterances.speaker: PW-035
utterances.text: The connection has to be made at the switchboard, and the switchboard operator sometimes waits for up to five minutes to connect, sometimes even ten minutes, before the conversation actually starts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So could it be missing from your intercept? Because within five minutes, a lot can be said. Could that be the difference between your intercept and the one of the other operator?

utterances.speaker: PW-035
utterances.text: Well, we never, between us, adjusted our clocks, the other operator and I.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: But tell me, is it possible that with a five-minute difference in timing, you record absolutely the same conversation?

utterances.speaker: PW-035
utterances.text: It could have easily, as I explained, at the same time. Only the clocks could have been out of sync by five minutes, although maybe another operator switched on only in the middle of the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you just say, for the transcript, whether the difference of five minutes is real between the other operator and you?

utterances.speaker: PW-035
utterances.text: I see here there is a five-minute difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So you think the difference is five minutes? Thank you. Yes or no? Thank you. Can you please just say that for the transcript?

utterances.speaker: PW-035
utterances.text: Yes, I see that there is a difference of five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please look on -- show on the screen 1D142, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did Ms. Stefanie Frease speak with you?

utterances.speaker: PW-035
utterances.text: Yes, she did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And did you give her a statement and sign a statement that you gave to her?

utterances.speaker: PW-035
utterances.text: Yes, I did sign a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you sign this paper that she's showing here as a report of the interview with you?

utterances.speaker: PW-035
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please show the signature of the witness on this document. If we can scroll up, please. Is there a version in the language the witness understands so that you can show it together with the document in English?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You can see both of these reports, and there is no signature anywhere. Can you tell us where your signature is?

utterances.speaker: PW-035
utterances.text: Well, I can't explain that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did the Prosecutor ever offer you or ask you to sign a statement?

utterances.speaker: PW-035
utterances.text: I don't remember if they did or didn't. Perhaps at the beginning, the first time that I came, but these last times that I came, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Is there another page of this document? Could we go to the last page? And it should not be broadcast. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We see that the document, this report on the conversation with you, was not signed in either version. Did you sign this or not?

utterances.speaker: PW-035
utterances.text: Since my signature is not on this document, then all I can say is that probably at that time I didn't sign it, because if I had signed it, the signature would be on the piece of paper. I don't see it here, if this is the original paper. If this is the original that was given to me by Ms. Frease, there is no signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe to us the difference between the antennas on the northern and southern locations? Was there a difference in antennas or did you have the same antennas?

utterances.speaker: PW-035
utterances.text: Sir, I think that our antennas were similar. At the southern location, we had additional stronger antennas, factory-produced ones, even, while at the northern location we, ourselves, made the antennas, and I think we only had one factory-built one. But the antennas were the same or similar, because they were received -- they were used for the receipt of -- for the reception of similar or same equipment used by the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In the Popovic case, in the summary of your testimony which was a bit more detailed than the one that was read to us here, on page 5457 said -- you said, I quote -- actually, the Prosecutor said, lines 8 and 9, transcript page 5457: "It was left up to them to decide, upon their own discretion, about the relevance of a document." Can you tell us, for the transcript, whose discretion was it that was a factor in deciding the relevance of a document?

utterances.speaker: PW-035
utterances.text: Operators, us, were allowed to decide that, but we were told what would constitute an important conversation. An important conversation was if new names appears on the lines, on the network, if an order of certain officers was recorded, picked up and recorded. If anything that we felt was important, except for family conversations by officers or just greetings, if anything new came up that we managed to hear and record, anything that was already not in our database at the centre, we would then decide to give that priority and send it on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just briefly, Mr. President. I think the witness understood the question after all, but the citation from the record was incorrect. The word "relevance of a given document" was used. It was "relevance of a given conversation," just so there's no confusion about whether we're talking about documents or conversations. And as I said, the witness understood the question, and that's what's important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please carry on, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. From what I recall, I asked the question about the relevance of the given transcript. Perhaps it was translated differently. But you know English so you can check that back in the transcript. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In order to finish with this question, which is not that relevant anyway, can you please tell us the criteria upon which you decided on the relevance of the intercepts? Were they mostly the conversation of the participants or something else?

utterances.speaker: PW-035
utterances.text: It was not only the conversation that was a deciding factor. The frequency also was important, if somebody was using a telephone that belonged to a known name of an officer. It wasn't a rule that it had to be done like that, but we would just pass it on if something new appeared that could help our database at the central centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Today, and also during your testimony in the Popovic case, the Prosecutor said that sometimes you did enter the date into the note-book, and sometimes you did not, and that it wasn't a problem if the date was not entered into the note-book because you believed that it was known, it was evident. Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: PW-035
utterances.text: Yes, it's true that we did not always enter the dates into the note-book.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us, why would the date of an intercept in the majority of cases not be entered into the note-book?

utterances.speaker: PW-035
utterances.text: The communications that we decided were important were sent for typing immediately, and the operator -- the typist who typed them in had to put the date in and send the document. So I wasn't really bothered by dates when I was writing in my own note-book. What was important was that the telegram had a date that was typed, and that was then sent to the central point.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you type the texts in the order in which they are in the note-book or did you first type out the more significant intercepts, followed by less significant ones?

utterances.speaker: PW-035
utterances.text: Yes, it's exactly the way you said. The most important intercepts were typed out immediately, while the others that we considered were not as important were typed out only at the end of the day and sent in the overall report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And did that affect the time when a certain intercept was recorded as having taken place or was this something that was done later?

utterances.speaker: PW-035
utterances.text: I don't know, really, whether this had an effect on the recorded time, but I can tell you that what we typed from the note-books, that was that, and it was the job of those in the database to deal further with that. So we didn't really bother to deal with that very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All right. Since you mentioned the note-books, can you please tell us whether these note-books were certified? Was there some sort of stamp or log number in them that was written? Was this done before the note-books were issued for use or was that done by the person who used the book?

utterances.speaker: PW-035
utterances.text: Actually, I don't remember exactly how that worked. The commander could probably tell you, the commander of the section that was entrusted with protocol matters and also who was in charge of collecting them once they were filled in, and then he would send them on to the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All right. Now we're talking about the note-books. You said that a sample of your handwriting was taken from you to see if that matched the handwriting in the books that you said you filled in. Was this sample ever examined by an expert, handwriting expert, and was it ever authenticated in some way?

utterances.speaker: PW-035
utterances.text: I know that I provided a sample of my handwriting. I don't know exactly which year. After that, nobody really told me anything about that. I think that some people were probably in charge of recognising or not recognising that particular handwriting sample.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In your first answer in the cross-examination today, you said that you used to type the documents and that another guy would type your transcripts in one case. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: PW-035
utterances.text: Yes. I also said that I typed in the intercepts into the computer on a couple of occasions because the person who usually did that wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So let us note there were several of you who typed in the intercepts at the southern location?

utterances.speaker: PW-035
utterances.text: Yes, there were at least two of us who did the typing.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, I apologise. Can we look at the note-book in e-court. This is Exhibit -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What is the number? We don't have it on the screen, for the sake of the record.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. P440. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We can see the note-book on the screen. I have it right now; I'm holding it in my hand. And you said that probably this was something that was agreed with them, just like we agreed that we would meet in 2001. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: PW-035
utterances.text: Well, it's just one of the endless possibilities. That doesn't have to be true at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. But does this perhaps refer to -- maybe is it possible that the generation of 2000, can they decide to -- decide something for generation 2001? Can generation 2000 meet in 2005 or 2006, or in reverse, 1994, 1995, 1996, 1997, 1998, 1999, 2000, 2001?

utterances.speaker: PW-035
utterances.text: Well, I don't know that. But I know that my high school class meets every 10 years, so I went on that basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what generation you are?

utterances.speaker: PW-035
utterances.text: Which generation, high school or some other school?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, it doesn't matter which school. Just can you give us any generation?

utterances.speaker: PW-035
utterances.text: I completed school in 1978.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So could we say that you are Generation 1978?

utterances.speaker: PW-035
utterances.text: I can say that for my high school graduation year.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Would it be possible, then, that you would publish, five years in advance, some slogan and that we would imprint them on booklets? By that time, you would already be enrolled in university or something like that?

utterances.speaker: PW-035
utterances.text: Well, I gave that answer as a possibility, one of countless possibilities, so what you are asking me is -- I mean, I can't even answer that. Would we do this, would we do that, would we do this five years in advance or not? I mean, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I apologise. Can you please tell us, for the transcript, whether this is note-book 22, and does it not state on it "1st Generation of 2001" on it?

utterances.speaker: PW-035
utterances.text: I can say that it says "1 GEN 2001," and this is marked as note-book 22.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would not wish to torture you any longer. Thank you very much for the answers you gave. I am thanking you on behalf of the Defence, and thank you for coming regardless of your current situation, despite of certain infirmities. Thank you for coming to testify. I wish you a safe trip, and may God bless you. And on behalf of the Defence, I would just like to say that we don't have any more questions for you. Your Honours, thank you very much. The Defence has completed its cross-examination of this witness. Thank you, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tolimir. Mr. Thayer, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Very briefly, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Witness, in the answer to one of the General's first questions -- he put upside by side two of the intercepts about Beara asking -- or complaining to General Krstic about not enough men, and in one of your answers you said that, if you remember correctly, the time on your intercept was "0957 hours."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we could just have P506A on the screen, just so that there's no confusion on the record. Again, that's P506A.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you see what's on the screen, sir? And if you do, can you identify what it is?

utterances.speaker: PW-035
utterances.text: Yes, I see I wrote here "1000," so it's 1000 hours, one 0 and then two small 0s. So it wasn't the way the gentleman said. I didn't have the document in front of me. I said that it was D57 [as interpreted], but actually what it says here now in front of me is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. I just wanted to clarify that. And, sir, do you read or speak any Italian, by any chance? Just very briefly.

utterances.speaker: PW-035
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: All right. No further questions for you at this time, then. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You will be pleased now this concludes your questioning, and you have the chance to return to your place of residence in a timely manner. Thank you for your attendance here and for the assistance you could give the Chamber and the parties. You are free now to return to your normal activities. Mr. Thayer, we are running out of time. How should we deal with the exhibits and the numbers? Could that be done perhaps by e-mail with the Registry?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think this is, for the time being, the best way to deal with it, or we deal with it, if necessary, during the next hearing. Thank you very much. We adjourn and resume next Tuesday in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 22nd day of June, 2010, at 2.15 p.m. 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.51 p.m.,
